prompt: A Quitanda analyst opens a file kept in Archive. How long does the first byte take to arrive?
hint: Compare the four classes on speed, not on price.

choices.text: Up to twelve hours, after a restore request
choices.why: That is how some archive tiers elsewhere work. Cloud Storage has no restore step for a class: Archive is read directly.

choices.text: Milliseconds, as in Standard
choices.why: Right. All four classes have the same latency and throughput; Archive differs in price and minimum stay.

choices.text: A few minutes, because the object is on slower disks
choices.why: Nothing about the class makes the read slower; the difference is the retrieval fee of 0.05 USD a GiB.

choices.text: It cannot be read until it is copied to Standard first
choices.why: Archive objects are read like any other. Copying it would itself pay the retrieval fee and a rewrite.

prompt: Quitanda writes 100 GiB to Coldline (0.007 USD per GiB-month, 90 days minimum) and deletes it after 30 days. Counting a month as 30 days, how many USD of storage is it billed in all?
hint: It is billed for the minimum, not for the days it stayed.

prompt: Match each class to its minimum storage duration.
hint: Each step colder roughly multiplies the stay.

prompt: Quitanda's app writes one 4 KB event per tap into Archive, 50 million of them a month. Which cost grows fastest with that design?
hint: Archive has no smallest billed size. Look at what is priced per request.

choices.text: The storage, because each 4 KB event is billed as 128 KiB
choices.why: Cloud Storage has no minimum object size: a 4 KB object is billed as 4 KB.

choices.text: The retrieval fee on writing them
choices.why: The retrieval fee is charged on reads, copies and rewrites, not on the upload.

choices.text: Class A operations, at 0.05 USD per 1,000 requests
choices.why: Right: 2,500 USD a month just to write them, for data that weighs about 200 GB.

choices.text: Nothing much, since Archive is the cheapest class
choices.why: It is the cheapest to keep per GiB, and the dearest per request.

prompt: An upload names no `--storage-class`. On Cloud Storage, which class does the object get?
hint: The bucket has a setting for exactly this.

choices.text: The bucket's default class
choices.why: Right, and a bucket created with no default has STANDARD.

choices.text: Always STANDARD, whatever the bucket says
choices.why: That is what fake-gcs-server does, ignoring the default; Cloud Storage uses the bucket's default class.

choices.text: NEARLINE, as the cheapest class without a long minimum
choices.why: Nothing picks a class by price; the bucket's default decides.

choices.text: The class of the last object written to that prefix
choices.why: Prefixes carry no settings; the bucket does.

prompt: A script uploads with `--storage-class=GLACIER`, and its tests against fake-gcs-server pass. What happens on Cloud Storage?
hint: Look at what the emulator did with a name it does not know.

choices.text: The object is stored as ARCHIVE, the nearest class
choices.why: Nothing translates names; Cloud Storage has no class called GLACIER and does not guess one.

choices.text: The upload is refused, because GLACIER is not one of its classes
choices.why: Right. The emulator stored the string as given, so the test proved nothing about the name.

choices.text: The object is stored as STANDARD with a warning
choices.why: Cloud Storage does not fall back silently; it refuses the request.

choices.text: It works, since the emulator imitates Cloud Storage's checks
choices.why: The emulator accepted a class Cloud Storage does not have, which is the point of the transcript.

prompt: Quitanda changes a Nearline object to Archive with `gcloud storage objects update --storage-class=ARCHIVE` ten days after writing it. What does Cloud Storage bill for the change?
hint: The flag triggers a rewrite.

choices.text: Nothing: a class change is a metadata edit
choices.why: Its help says it triggers a rewrite of the object's data, which is a new object.

choices.text: Only the difference in storage price between the two classes from that day on, prorated
choices.why: That leaves out what the rewrite itself costs.

choices.text: A Class A operation, a retrieval fee, and Nearline's 20 remaining days
choices.why: Right. A rewrite reads the old object, writes a new one, and ends the old one's life early.

choices.text: A Class B operation, because the object is read
choices.why: A rewrite is a write, billed as Class A at the destination class's rate.

prompt: In `gcloud storage objects describe`, after `objects update --storage-class`, a different ___ number shows that a new object was written over the old one.
hint: It is the number written after `#` in an object's full address.

prompt: Which command restores an object stored in Archive so that it can be read?
hint: Read the help of `gcloud storage restore` again.

choices.text: `gcloud storage restore`
choices.why: That command restores soft-deleted objects, which is a different thing.

choices.text: `gcloud storage objects update --storage-class=STANDARD`
choices.why: That rewrites the object into Standard, paying the retrieval fee; it is not needed to read it.

choices.text: None is needed; just read it
choices.why: Right. `cat` or `cp` reads it at once, and the retrieval fee is charged on the bytes served.

choices.text: `gcloud storage cp` with a restore tier
choices.why: There are no restore tiers in Cloud Storage's classes.

prompt: A report reads 300 GiB from Coldline objects (retrieval 0.02 USD per GiB). Leaving out operations and network, what is the retrieval fee, in USD?
hint: The fee is per GiB served.

prompt: A program reads only the first 8 MB of each 100 MB Nearline object, and a download sometimes breaks halfway. On what is the retrieval fee charged?
hint: The pricing page talks about the data accessed.

choices.text: On the bytes actually served
choices.why: Right: 8 MB for the partial read, and whatever arrived before the break.

choices.text: On the whole object, 100 MB, every time it is opened
choices.why: The pricing page says the fee is based on the data accessed, not on the size of the object.

choices.text: On nothing, since a partial read is a Class B operation only
choices.why: The operation is charged as well; the fee still applies to the bytes read.

choices.text: On the object's size, but only once a month
choices.why: There is no monthly cap or charge per object; it is per byte served.

prompt: In a bucket with Autoclass, what happens to an object that is read after 200 days in Coldline?
hint: Autoclass follows how each object is used, in both directions.

choices.text: It stays in Coldline and pays the retrieval fee
choices.why: Autoclass buckets pay no retrieval fees, and a read moves the object.

choices.text: It moves back to Standard
choices.why: Right. A read returns it to Standard, and it starts ageing again from there.

choices.text: It moves on to Archive, the terminal class
choices.why: Ageing only happens while an object is not read.

choices.text: It is restored first and then read
choices.why: No class in Cloud Storage needs a restore.

prompt: Quitanda's data lake bucket has Autoclass and 2 million objects of 50 MiB each, kept the whole month. At 0.0025 USD per 1,000 objects per 30 days, what is the month's management fee, in USD?
hint: The fee is per object, whatever its size, once it is 128 KiB or more.

prompt: Quitanda's logs are written as one 20 KiB object per request. Why does Autoclass save nothing on them?
hint: Look at the size below which Autoclass does nothing.

choices.text: Autoclass refuses buckets that hold small objects
choices.why: It accepts them; it just leaves them where they are.

choices.text: Objects under 128 KiB are not managed: they stay in Standard
choices.why: Right. They pay no fee and never move; writing fewer, larger objects is the first fix.

choices.text: The fee on each 20 KiB object costs more than the object's storage
choices.why: Objects under 128 KiB are not charged the fee at all.

choices.text: Logs are read too often in their first week to ever leave Standard
choices.why: That may be true for a week; the reason here is the size, which keeps them out whatever the reads.

prompt: At 0.007 USD per GiB-month, what does a tebibyte (1,024 GiB) cost to keep in Coldline for a year, in USD?
hint: Volume times monthly price times twelve.

prompt: A tebibyte is kept a full year in São Paulo and read back whole about ten times. Which class does the lesson's arithmetic make cheapest?
hint: Archive stops winning at 1.6 reads, Nearline only starts at 15.6.

choices.text: Archive
choices.why: Archive stops being cheaper than Coldline at 1.6 full reads a year.

choices.text: Nearline
choices.why: Nearline only beats Coldline from 15.6 full reads a year.

choices.text: Coldline
choices.why: Right: from about 1.6 to 15.6 full reads a year, Coldline is the cheapest of the four.

choices.text: Standard
choices.why: Standard only wins above about 18 full reads a year.

prompt: Quitanda keeps a scratch tebibyte for 60 days and never reads it. Why is Archive, the cheapest line of the table, the wrong class for it?
hint: The table assumes every object stays a full year.

choices.text: Archive objects cannot be deleted at all until their first year has passed
choices.why: They can be deleted whenever you like; the bill is what follows the delete.

choices.text: Archive bills a full 365 days, so 60 days cost 37.38 USD, not about 6
choices.why: Right. Coldline, at 90 days minimum, bills 21.50 USD here, the cheapest of the four.

choices.text: Reading it back from Archive would take longer than the 60 days allow
choices.why: Nothing in Cloud Storage takes long to read, and this data is never read.

choices.text: Archive is only offered in multi-regions
choices.why: Archive exists in São Paulo, at 0.003 USD a GiB-month.

prompt: Match each kind of Quitanda data to the class that fits it.
hint: Ask how often it is read and how long it is kept.

pairs.left: Today's orders, read by every report
Delivery photos read only when a customer disputes an order, kept two years
A monthly snapshot read by finance once or twice in the year after it is taken
Backups restored for a test every few weeks and kept three months

prompt: Order the classes by the fee for reading a GiB back, cheapest first.
hint: Standard charges nothing; the floor of the keeping price is the ceiling of this one.

prompt: Against fake-gcs-server, a test writes an object with `--storage-class=COLDLINE`, rewrites it to ARCHIVE, and checks the class. What does the test prove?
hint: Look at what the emulator returned after the rewrite.

choices.text: That rewrites keep the class, since the emulator answered COLDLINE
choices.why: The emulator answered STANDARD after every rewrite, whatever was asked.

choices.text: That the request was well formed, and nothing about the stored class
choices.why: Right. The emulator writes every rewritten object as Standard, so the class it reports is its own.

choices.text: That Cloud Storage would refuse the rewrite inside the 90-day minimum
choices.why: Cloud Storage allows it and bills the rest of the 90 days; the emulator bills nothing.

choices.text: That the Archive retrieval fee was charged
choices.why: Nothing is billed in the emulator, and the fee would be Coldline's anyway.
